Welcome toMean Energy in a Well

A bead jiggles in a warm well — how much energy does it hold on average?

How would you like to begin?

Listen to the intro

About: the mean potential energy of a thermally jostled bead in wells of different shape and stiffness

Source

Concept
A bead in a one-dimensional well E = b|q|n, in contact with surroundings at T = 300 K. The sim measures its time-averaged potential energy Ē, its root-mean-square displacement qrms and the distribution of its energy, for n = 1, 2 and 4 and for widths ℓ from 50 nm to 200 nm.
Serves
Equipartition of energy (Fermi Notes, §4.5, eqs 4.65–4.66): where its numerical factor comes from.
Inquiry
Five subject-expert questions, each answered by measurement (the running-average chart, the energy histogram and the Readouts panel), and a closing summary card.
Misconception
Common intuitions about how a jostled bead shares energy with its surroundings; each is addressed in the feedback only after the student has committed to an answer.
Model
Metropolis rule on x = q/ℓ with u = E/kBT = 6|x|n: trial step 0.5(2r − 1), accepted if u does not rise or with probability e−Δu. 200 steps per frame; 12 000 steps are counted as 1 s. Positions are continuous (classical limit); only potential energy is averaged. The bead's kinetic energy, quadratic in its velocity, would add ½kBT in every well. kB = 1.380649×10−23 J/K, so kBT = 4.142 zJ.
Controls
Well shape (bq², b|q|, bq⁴) and width ℓ, defined so that E(±ℓ) = 6kBT, i.e. b = 6kBT/ℓn. Changing either restarts the run from q = 0; the previous run's chart trace stays in grey and its numbers stay in the Previous run card of the Readouts panel. ↻ Reset clears both.

Pedagogy principles applied

PrincipleHow this sim honors it
Commit, then checkEach SME question is a gated choice card; the sim boots paused with every readout at —, so the student can commit to an answer before pressing Play.
Measurement, not formulaNo formula for Ē and no line at any special energy is drawn; values are read from the running average, its chart and the energy histogram.
Stable scalesEnergy axis fixed at 0–7 kBT, q axis at ±240 nm, histogram at 0–1, chart at 0–30 s and 0–1.5; narrowing ℓ visibly squeezes the well.
Compare by contrastThe trace of the run just ended stays on the chart in grey and its numbers in the Previous run readouts, so two shapes or widths are compared side by side.
Readout disciplineThe Readouts panel, below the controls, always shows t and Ē; qrms and the share of steps below 0.5kBT appear with the questions that use them, and everything shows in free exploration.
Real values, labelled scalingT = 300 K, kBT = 4.142 zJ, q in nm; the simulated clock (12 000 steps = 1 s) is stated in the chart title.
Honest animationLike a strobe photograph of a trapped Brownian bead, the bead appears at a fresh sampled position each frame, with faint copies of its last 30 positions.
Mean Energy and the Shape of a Well
Bead in the well E(q) and its energy histogram
Running average Ē / kBT against time · 12 000 steps = 1 s

Guided Inquiry

1 · The parabolic well

The page opens with the parabolic well at ℓ = 200 nm. Press Play and watch the bead and the running average until t passes 30 s. Where does Ē settle?

2 · The V-shaped well

Switch the well shape to V-shaped, keeping ℓ = 200 nm, and watch until t passes 30 s. The Previous run readouts keep the parabolic result. Where does Ē settle now?

3 · A stiffer well

Keep the V-shaped well at ℓ = 200 nm and let t pass 30 s. Then set ℓ = 50 nm, a well four times stiffer, and watch until t passes 30 s again; the Previous run readouts keep the 200 nm values. How do qrms and Ē change?

4 · The quartic well

Switch the well shape to quartic, set ℓ = 200 nm and watch until t passes 30 s. Where does Ē settle?

5 · Comparing the histograms

Set ℓ = 200 nm and switch between the parabolic and the V-shaped wells, letting each run for at least 10 s and watching the energy histogram and the lowest-band readout. What difference between the two histograms accounts for the smaller Ē of the parabolic well?

6 · What the wells show

For a well E = b|q|n the average potential energy is kBT/n: 1.00, 0.50 and 0.25kBT for the V-shaped, parabolic and quartic wells, whatever the width ℓ. The width sets only the spread: qrms is proportional to ℓ.

So the ½kBT of equipartition is not a rule for every coordinate. It belongs to energies quadratic in a coordinate. The bead's kinetic energy, ½mv², is quadratic in v, so it holds ½kBT on average in any well; this sim tracks only the potential energy.

Mean Energy and the Shape of a Well

✦Learn this with the AI tutor

01

At a glance

A small bead sits in a one-dimensional well while its surroundings, at 300 K, keep kicking it. This sim follows the bead's potential energy as it wanders, and reports its average Ē, its spread qrms and a histogram of the energies it visits.

What you'll learn

  • How the Boltzmann weight e−E/kBT decides how often the bead is found at each energy.
  • How the average energy Ē depends on the shape of the well, E = b|q|n, and on its width ℓ.
  • How to read Ē, qrms and the share of steps below 0.5 kBT from the readouts and the histogram.
  • Where the equipartition result in the notes comes from, and what it needs.
The set-up: three wells that all reach 6 kBT at q = ±ℓ, and a bead that the surroundings keep kicking.

What's on screen

  • Grey line (top left): the well E(q), with E in units of kBT. The orange bead is the system, and its fading dots are its last few positions.
  • Dashed orange line: the running average Ē, drawn across the well.
  • Blue bars (top right): the energy histogram, the fraction of steps spent in each 0.5 kBT band.
  • Orange trace (bottom): Ē/kBT against run time t, over 30 s. A grey trace keeps the previous run.
  • Readouts: t, Ē, qrms and the share below 0.5 kBT, for this run and the previous one.
See itStart the bead again from q = 0 with your current well. Watch for: the bead being kicked about the well, the histogram filling in and the orange trace being drawn below.

03

A parabolic well holds ½ kBT

At temperature T the chance of finding the bead at energy E is weighted by the Boltzmann factor e−βE, with β = 1/kBT. The mean energy is the average of E over that weight. The notes work it out for E = bq², where q is one coordinate.

Notes (4.65) and (4.66). The Gaussian integrals leave b/2βb, so b cancels.

The result is Ē = ½kBT, which is 2.07 zJ at 300 K, however stiff the parabola is. The bead is found most often near the bottom, but it is not frozen there: the kicks keep lifting it, and the mean settles at half of kBT.

The derivation replaces a sum over states by an integral, so it needs the levels to be closely spaced compared with kBT. The sim treats positions as continuous, which is that limit.

See itOpen the parabolic well at your width. Watch for: the dashed line and the orange trace settling at 0.50 kBT (2.07 zJ) as the run passes about 10 s.
04

A V-shaped well holds a full kBT

The same recipe for E = b|q| (notes, problems after §4.5, no. 3) uses integrals over positive q only, and b again cancels.

Average of b|q| with the weight e−βb|q|: a whole kBT, twice the parabolic value.

The V has a narrow bottom, which is why its mean is twice the parabola's: only a short stretch of q has a low energy, so the bead spends less of its time there. In the sim, the lowest band, below 0.5 kBT, holds about 0.39 of the V's steps, against about 0.68 for the parabola.

For the V the stretch of q per unit of energy is the same at every energy. The histogram therefore falls off as e−E/kBT alone, and the mean of that falls at kBT.

See itOpen the V-shaped well at your width. Watch for: Ē settling at 1.00 kBT (4.14 zJ), with the share below 0.5 kBT near 0.39.
05

The power of q sets the mean: kBT/n

For E = b|q|n, the range of q with energy below E has length proportional to E1/n. The number of positions per unit of energy therefore goes as E1/n−1, and the Boltzmann weight multiplies it.

The integrals are gamma functions, Γ(1/n + 1) and Γ(1/n), and Γ(x + 1) = xΓ(x) leaves 1/n.

So n = 1, 2 and 4 give 1.00, 0.50 and 0.25 kBT. A flatter bottom, a larger n, leaves more room at low energy, so the bead spends more of its time there and the mean is lower. In the sim about 0.85 of the quartic's steps are below 0.5 kBT.

The range of q below energy E, as a fraction of its value at 6 kBT. At 0.5 kBT it is 0.08, 0.29 and 0.54 for n = 1, 2 and 4.
See itOpen the quartic well at your width. Watch for: Ē settling at 0.25 kBT (1.04 zJ), with the share below 0.5 kBT near 0.85.
06

The width sets only the spread

Narrowing ℓ shrinks every length by the same factor, and b = 6 kBT/ℓn grows to match. The Boltzmann weight depends on the energy alone, so the bead visits each energy as often as before, and Ē does not move. Only the spread qrms changes, in proportion to ℓ.

The same V at ℓ = 200 nm and 50 nm. Every distance falls by four, and the energies do not change.

For the V, qrms goes from 47.1 nm at 200 nm to 11.8 nm at 50 nm. At 200 nm the parabola has qrms = 57.7 nm and the quartic 74.3 nm.

The quartic wanders furthest because its flat bottom lets it move far at little cost in energy. A large qrms does not mean a large Ē.

See itOpen the V-shaped well at ℓ = 50 nm. Watch for: qrms reading about 12 nm while Ē still settles at 1.00 kBT.
07

Where it matters

  • Atoms in a gas. Each velocity component adds a quadratic term ½mv², worth ½kBT. Three components give &frac32;kBT per atom (notes, §1.2 and §4.5). The bead's own kinetic energy would add ½kBT in every well; the sim tracks the potential energy only.
  • Optical tweezers. A bead held in a laser trap sits in a parabolic well. Its position spread gives the stiffness: with E = bq² the notes' result says b·⟨q²⟩ = ½kBT.
  • Where equipartition fails. When the energy levels are not close together compared with kBT, as for the vibration of a small molecule at room temperature, the integral is a poor stand-in for the sum and the mean falls short.
08

Summary

In one line. The bead's energy is weighted by the Boltzmann factor e−E/kBT, and the sim's Ē and qrms are averages over that weight.

Key points

  • For E = b|q|n, Ē = kBT/n: 1.00, 0.50 and 0.25 kBT for n = 1, 2 and 4.
  • The constant b, and so the width ℓ, cancels from Ē.
  • qrms is proportional to ℓ, and is largest for the quartic well.

Common mix-ups

  • “The bead sits at the bottom, so its energy is zero.” It is found most often low, but the kicks keep lifting it: the parabola averages 0.50 kBT.
  • “Equipartition gives ½kBT in every well.” Only for an energy quadratic in q. The V gives 1.00 kBT and the quartic 0.25 kBT.
  • “A narrower well lowers the average energy.” It lowers qrms, from 47.1 nm to 11.8 nm for the V, and leaves Ē at 1.00 kBT.

Things to try on your own

  • Run each shape at 200 nm for 30 s, multiply Ē by n, and note that every product is kBT.
  • Run the V at 200 nm and then at 100 nm, and compare the two qrms readouts with the factor of two in ℓ.
  • For each shape, read the share below 0.5 kBT after 30 s and compare it with 0.39, 0.68 and 0.85.
